movune.headline: Organizing a complex product before implementation.
movune.lead: Movune is an evolving personal project: a B2B SaaS designed to support the management of physiotherapy and Pilates clinics in Brazil. The case study documents the decisions and product development process.
movune.role: Product definition, flows, screen architecture, UI/UX direction, and prototyping.

overview.title: Overview
overview.context: The product aims to centralize management activities for physiotherapy and Pilates clinics. The considered domain includes schedules, patients, appointments, classes, packages, finance, documents, and communication, as well as distinct operational rules.
overview.challenge: The challenge was to organize a broad idea into a coherent product structure and validate the experience before defining production architecture.

process.title: Process
process.introduction: The work moved through connected stages, keeping decisions and prototype aligned.
process.productDescription: Organizing the problem, audience, and considered domain.
process.flowsDescription: Mapping relevant journeys, rules, and exceptions.
process.architectureDescription: Structuring navigation and relationships between modules.
process.interfaceDescription: Visual direction and the states needed to make flows legible.
process.prototypeDescription: Validating decisions early and identifying inconsistencies.

interface.title: Interface
interface.description: The schedule brings individual appointments and classes into the same context. During scheduling, supporting actions — such as registering a patient who does not exist yet — happen without leaving the flow or losing data already entered.
interface.scheduleAlt: Movune desktop schedule in the light theme, with individual appointments and classes in the same context.
interface.mobileAlt: Quick patient registration in Movune’s scheduling flow, in a mobile layout and light theme.
interface.compareTitle: Light and dark as part of the same system
interface.compareDescription: Both themes preserve the same hierarchy, states, and interaction structure. The adaptation is not just a color inversion: surfaces, contrast, and functional elements still need to remain readable in both contexts.
interface.compareLightAlt: Movune patients interface in the light theme with quick registration open.
interface.compareDarkAlt: Movune patients interface in the dark theme with quick registration open.

decisions.title: Key decisions
decisions.introduction: The decisions below belong to product definition and prototyping; they do not describe implemented functionality.
decisions.scheduleDescription: Both contexts require their own rules and readings instead of one generic flow.
decisions.recurrenceDescription: Recurring appointments need to make exceptions and overlaps explicit.
decisions.statusDescription: The operational state and appointment state are related but distinct information.
decisions.registrationDescription: Scheduling can open an essential registration step and return to the original flow.

status.description: Movune remains in prototyping. Product definition, the main flows, screen architecture, and visual identity already have a consolidated direction, while the prototype continues to be refined before production architecture is defined and implementation begins.

rigset.headline: Configure and manage your workstation, your way.
rigset.lead: An open-source CLI to define, configure, and manage the state of a workstation in a declarative, secure, and predictable way.
rigset.note: Product, architecture, CLI experience, and v1 roadmap are defined. Implementation has not started yet.
rigset.caption: Conceptual visual — not the final interface.
rigset.overviewAlt: Conceptual visual of Rigset. It does not represent the final interface.

problem.title: Configuring a workstation is more than installing tools.
problem.p1: A workstation accumulates applications, command-line tools, runtimes, versions, configurations, files, services, and preferences. These resources may come from different origins, already exist before any management tool, and be distributed across distinct environments, such as Windows and WSL.
problem.p2: Reproducing or maintaining that environment is not just a matter of installing what is missing. It is necessary to understand what already exists, where it exists, how it was configured, and which changes can be made without overwriting decisions or resources that do not belong to the tool.
problem.p3: Rigset starts from this problem: allowing the user to describe how they want their workstation and bringing the current state closer to that desired state without treating the entire machine as something that can be changed freely.
problem.versionQ: Is it at the expected version?
problem.environmentQ: Is it in the correct environment?
problem.close: The challenge is not to automate more changes. It is knowing which changes should happen — and which should not.

proposal.title: Manage state, not just run installations.
proposal.p1: Rigset treats workstation configuration as a reconciliation process. The user defines the desired state, Rigset observes the current reality, and, from that context, builds an explicit plan to bring the two closer together.
proposal.p2: That difference, however, is not enough to authorize changes. Planning also considers where each resource exists, what Rigset is permitted to manage, its compatibility, and the available evidence before deciding what can be done.
proposal.p3: The result is a flow in which observing, planning, executing, and verifying are distinct stages — and no change should happen simply because a difference was found.
proposal.desiredText: How does the user want the workstation to be?
proposal.authorityText: What is Rigset authorized to change?
proposal.compatibilityText: Is this change valid in this environment?
proposal.evidenceText: Is there enough evidence to trust this conclusion?
proposal.plan: Before any mutation, Rigset produces a deterministic, explainable plan with the necessary actions, conflicts, privileges, risks, and relevant known effects.
proposal.planCallout: Every mutating operation must have a non-mutating planning path.
proposal.apply: Rigset executes only the approved changes. If the reality encountered during execution materially invalidates the plan, it does not improvise a different intent.
proposal.verify: An operation is only considered complete after the resulting state is observed again. A command finishing successfully is not, by itself, proof that the desired result was achieved.
proposal.close2: Rigset manages what the user entrusts to it, not the entire machine.

model.title: A machine can contain more than one environment.
model.p1: A workstation does not need to be treated as a single homogeneous environment. A Windows machine, for example, can run tools natively and also have different distributions in WSL, each with its own versions, configurations, providers, and state.
model.p2: Rigset represents these contexts as independent Target Environments within the same Machine. This makes it possible to observe, evaluate, and manage each environment without assuming that the state found in one of them also applies to the others.
model.tree:
Machine
├ Windows Native
├ WSL Ubuntu
└ WSL Arch
model.instanceTitle: The same resource does not mean the same instance
model.instance: For Rigset, Git is a Canonical Resource: the logical identity of the resource it knows. But each occurrence of that resource within a Target Environment is an independent Resource Instance.
model.formula: CANONICAL RESOURCE + TARGET ENVIRONMENT = RESOURCE INSTANCE
model.unequal: Git on Windows ≠ Git on WSL Ubuntu
model.independent: Same resource. Independent contexts and states.
model.targetFirst: Rigset first resolves where the resource should exist. Only then does it choose how that resource can be observed or managed in that environment.

security.title: Finding a difference does not mean having permission to fix it.
security.intro1: Rigset can discover software, configurations, and differences between the current and desired state without assuming that those resources belong to it.
security.intro2: Detecting a resource does not create ownership. Finding drift does not authorize overwriting a configuration. And removing something from Rigset’s configuration does not mean the corresponding software should be uninstalled.
security.intro3: Automation only proceeds when there is management authority compatible with the planned change and, when the action is consequential, explicit user consent.
security.trustTitle: Rigset manages only what has been entrusted to it
security.trust1: An already existing resource can be observed without being managed. For Rigset to assume responsibility over it, the user needs to perform an explicit adoption, preserving its origin and choosing which kinds of change will be authorized.
security.trust2: That authority can be limited. Allowing Rigset to manage a configuration, for example, does not automatically grant permission to install, update, or uninstall the resource.
security.automationCallout: Automation removes repetition, not consequential decisions.
security.recovery: Rigset does not assume that every change on the workstation can be reverted transactionally. When an operation fails partially, it preserves what actually happened, observes the current state again, and uses that reality to build the next safe plan.
security.recoveryCallout: Accurate recovery is more important than magical rollback.
security.privacy: Rigset’s essential operation is local-first. Observing the workstation does not authorize transmitting its data, and the Core does not depend on telemetry. In v1, telemetry is zero by default.

catalog.title: A small catalog to prove different problems.
catalog.intro1: Rigset’s v1 does not aim to support as many tools as possible. The initial catalog is deliberately small to validate, end to end, the Core’s most important properties.
catalog.intro2: Git, Node.js, and VS Code with extensions were chosen as Reference Resources because they present different management problems. Together, they exercise reconciliation, ownership, versions, PATH, multiple environments, desktop applications, and child resources without requiring a broad catalog before those abstractions have been proven.
catalog.vscodeTree:
Desktop app
├ CLI
└ Extensions
   ├ declared
   ├ missing
   └ external → preserve
catalog.depth: Each catalog resource should expose only capabilities it actually has. Core abstractions should emerge from the differences found in these concrete cases — not from universal interfaces created in advance for hypothetical resources.
catalog.slices: Development will be done in vertical slices. Each slice starts with a claim about Rigset’s behavior, defines what evidence is needed to prove it, and implements only what is necessary to produce that proof.

status.title: Planned in depth. Not yet implemented.
status.intro1: Rigset does not yet have a functional implementation. The work so far has focused on defining the product, modeling the domain, establishing the security limits, and designing an implementation and validation strategy before starting the Core.
status.intro2: These definitions form the initial contract of v1, but some technical decisions remain deliberately open and will need to be resolved with evidence during implementation.
status.languageText: The language will be chosen before Core implementation. Until that decision is made, Go and Rust are not presented as technologies used in the project.
status.expand: Expand proofs with Node.js and VS Code

overtime.headline: Reply fast, without accepting what does not fit the schedule.
overtime.lead: Automation that identifies overtime opportunities in messages, checks the user’s schedule, availability, and configured limits, and replies automatically when the opportunity is eligible.
overtime.note: The problem, main rules, and initial decision flow are defined. Technical requirements and implementation have not started yet.

problem.title: When the first to reply gets the opportunity, watching the group becomes part of the work.
problem.p1: Overtime opportunities can be posted in WhatsApp groups and assigned to whoever replies first. For anyone interested in accepting them, that means constantly watching the messages and reacting quickly.
problem.p2: But speed is not the only criterion. An opportunity may coincide with the regular schedule, conflict with another overtime already accepted, occur in a period when the user is unavailable, or exceed an allowed overtime limit.
problem.p3: The decision, therefore, is not simply “reply first,” but “reply first when the opportunity can actually be accepted.”
problem.scenario: In the scenario that originated the project, opportunities are posted in natural language, indicating information such as role, group, date, and period — not always with an explicit time.
problem.example: I need someone in [role] for group [X] tonight.
problem.close: Speed when there is certainty. Abstention when there is ambiguity.

decision.title: Replying is the last step, not the first.
decision.p1: Each new message needs to be interpreted and checked against the user’s current context. The automation only replies when it can identify the opportunity and verify that all known conditions allow accepting it.
decision.p2: If a required piece of information is missing, ambiguous, or cannot be verified safely, no automatic reply is sent.
decision.interpret: Interpret: turn natural language into a structured opportunity.
decision.role: Role: only eligible roles configured for the user.
decision.group: Group: information from the opportunity and the record. Additional eligibility criteria by group remain open.
decision.schedule: Schedule: check for conflict with the regular schedule.
decision.unavailabilityText: Unavailability: recurring; one-off; full day or period.
decision.conflictsText: Conflicts: already accepted overtime also blocks.
decision.limitText: Limit: configurable maximum. The initial scenario uses 3 acceptances/month only as an example, not as a universal product rule.
decision.respond: Reply: use a simple, predefined message — “I accept,” “I can,” or “I’m available.” Do not use AI-generated text.
decision.record: Record structured data: date; period/time; role; group; reply sent; acceptance time; status.
decision.evidence: Preserve the original message separately as context and evidence.
decision.notify: Notify: every automatic acceptance must be communicated to the user.
decision.rule: Without reliable information → do not reply.

rules.title: Automating the reply requires knowing the limits.
rules.outside: Outside the schedule and without restrictions → available by default.
rules.close3: When in doubt, do not accept.

limits.title: The behavior is taking shape. The implementation is not yet.
limits.p1: The concept already defines the problem, the main decision flow, and the rules that determine when an opportunity can be accepted automatically.
limits.p2: Architecture, stack, and the integration mechanisms needed to turn this behavior into a working system have not been defined yet. Some rules of the domain itself also need to be deepened before implementation.

status.title: A real problem turned into a structured concept.
status.p1: The project is still in the concept phase. The work so far has focused on understanding the problem, turning the initial scenario into explicit rules, and structuring the flow needed to decide when an opportunity can be accepted automatically.
status.p2: Before implementation, it is still necessary to deepen the requirements, validate the integrations involved, and define the technical and security decisions that will support the automation.
status.next: Turn the current concept into detailed requirements, first investigating the constraints of the WhatsApp and schedule-source integrations before defining architecture and technologies.
